Bayer Leverkusen · Bundesliga 2023-24

Unbeaten

Colin Spelman · Built on Hudl StatsBomb free event and 360 data · October 2026

28 wins, 6 draws, 0 losses. 90 points, 89 goals scored, 24 conceded. This is how Xabi Alonso's side did it, told through every one of their 78 non-penalty goals and five questions about how they played.

Watch the goals

Every goal below is rebuilt from data. Leverkusen are in red, opponents in white. Every touch of the ball is placed at its recorded location and time. Everyone else comes from StatsBomb's 360 freeze frames, which capture every player the broadcast camera could see at each on-ball event, with movement between frames smoothed.

Each goal opens in a 3D game view: a broadcast-style camera behind the attack, with every tracked player rendered as a 3D footballer in team colours with his shirt number, running, turning and leaning according to the data. The player on the ball is placed exactly where each event happened, so passes arrive at the receiver's feet and carries keep the ball with the carrier. Passes travel on the ground or in the air by StatsBomb's recorded pass height. The figures are generic, not likenesses; the camera, kits and stadium are styling and the positions underneath are the data. Switch to tactical view for the top-down version.

1. How were the goals built?

Leverkusen's goals came from longer moves than the goals they conceded. The median Leverkusen goal followed 6 passes in the same possession, against 2.5 for their opponents. 29% of their goals came after 10 or more passes, and 46% started in their own half. They could also score quickly: 31% came after 2 passes or fewer, mostly set pieces and counters.

2. Who made it tick?

Granit Xhaka was involved in 29% of Leverkusen's 20,174 completed open-play passes, as passer or receiver. No one else was above 18%. The network shows the shape: a back three, Xhaka and a partner in midfield, wingbacks Grimaldo and Frimpong stretched wide, and Wirtz and Hofmann between the lines.

3. Who broke the lines, and who received?

Using 360 freeze frames, I counted a pass as line-breaking if it was completed, gained at least 10 yards and went past at least 3 visible outfield opponents. Leverkusen played 84 of these per match, against 47 for their opponents. The rate per completed pass was about the same (17.8% vs 18.4%): the gap is volume, because they had the ball far more.

The roles split cleanly. Xhaka played 15.8 line-breaking passes per 90, the most in the squad. The players receiving them were the wingbacks and the two attacking midfielders: Frimpong, Wirtz (16.5 per 90) and Hofmann.

4. Were the late goals luck?

Take away Leverkusen's goals from the 85th minute on and the season changes: 10 fewer points and 4 defeats. There is no unbeaten season without them.

So was it luck? Partly, but not mostly. The chances were real: minutes 75 to 85 were Leverkusen's most dangerous spell of any match period (2.74 xG per 90), and the final minutes ran at 2.40, level with their first-half peak. They also finished well above that: 13 goals from 8.8 xG after the 85th minute. The pressure looks like a repeatable habit. Scoring about 4 more late goals than the chances deserved is the part you'd bet against happening again.

5. Where did they win the ball back?

28% of Leverkusen's ball regains came in the attacking third, against 16% for their opponents. That is 577 high regains across the season, 17 a match. About a third of them (35%) led to a shot within 15 seconds, the same rate as their opponents (34%). The edge was not converting high regains better. It was having nearly twice as many.

What travels from this

Three things a recruitment or analysis team could take from the season. Possession volume, not efficiency, was the edge: line-breaking rate and high-regain conversion were average, the amount was not. The midfield ran through one player to an unusual degree, which is a strength until he's missing. And the late-goal run was built on real pressure but finished at a rate that should be expected to cool.

Method and limits

Data: Hudl StatsBomb free release of all 34 Leverkusen Bundesliga matches, 2023-24: events, lineups and 360 freeze frames. Only Leverkusen's matches are included, so every baseline is "their opponents in the same games", not the league.

Animations: ball path from event locations, end points and timestamps; players from 360 frames and the named shot freeze frame. The player on the ball is identified at every event; other dots are linked between frames by minimum-distance matching with a speed limit, starting from the named shot frame and working backwards. Players off camera for more than 3 seconds fade out instead of being shown on an invented path. Unnamed Leverkusen dots appear lighter.

Definitions: line-breaking pass = completed open-play pass, 10+ yards forward, past 3+ visible outfield opponents (camera coverage means this undercounts). Regain = successful ball recovery, interception or won tackle. xG = StatsBomb's model.

Code: Python (NumPy, SciPy for the assignment step) and three.js for the 3D view. Full source and run instructions on GitHub.
